title: The last canto
about: Dante has risen to the last heaven, one of pure light, where the blessed form a white rose. Beatrice, who led him up, is back in her seat among them, and Saint Bernard, devoted to the Virgin Mary, stands beside him. The canto opens with Bernard’s prayer to her that Dante may be given the strength to see God; the prayer is granted, and the rest is what he saw. He is, he says, like a man after a dream: the feeling stays and the sight is almost gone.

view.says: For Auden, Dante is the greatest writer of dream literature: his images never run dry, and his exact structure of logic and mathematics fixes even the number of lines. For Dante, he wrote, the vision of one beloved person’s glory is not the foot of a long ladder: a single step leads from it to God, and in the last vision that love is transformed, not destroyed.
view.quote: there is only one step to take, from the personal creature who can love and be loved to the personal Creator who is Love
view.source: “George Macdonald” (1954) and the Introduction to *The Protestant Mystics* (1964), both in *Forewords and Afterwords* (1973), pp. 269 and 68
view.checked: read in the scan of Forewords and Afterwords, research/auden/fa.txt: lines 12831-12840 (in this scan the page number follows the text of its page; 269 stands at line 12856) and lines 3238-3244 (68 stands at line 3253); the Vision of Eros is defined at lines 2984-2988. The scan drops most punctuation and prints the word is in capitals, which appears to stand for an italic; the quotation keeps the scan's one comma.

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: paradox
lenses.plain: a statement that contradicts itself on the surface and is still meant as true
lenses.caption: The prayer opens with three pairs of terms, and each pair is one name for Mary: Vergine Madre, virgin mother; figlia del tuo figlio, daughter of your son; umile e alta, lowly and high. By the measure of nature the two terms of each pair contradict each other. A statement that contradicts itself and is true all the same is a paradox. Pairs like these were already a formula of the Church’s public prayer. The next three lines state the event they point to: she raised human nature so high that its maker did not disdain to become its creature. In the faith the poem holds, each pair is fact.
lenses.why: The three paradoxes name Mary by the event the next lines state outright: in her the maker of human nature became its creature. Such pairs were a formula of the Church’s prayer, and in the poem’s faith each is fact.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and lines 4 to 6. Paradox as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. That the pairs contradict by nature’s measure and hold in faith, that such pairs were a formula of the liturgy, and that all three point to the event of lines 4 to 6: the notes on these lines by Sapegno, Singleton, Bosco and Reggio, and Chiavacci Leonardi, read at the Dartmouth Dante Project.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: Lines 1 and 3 rhyme. The line between them ends on creatura, creature, and lines 4 and 6 answer it with natura, nature, and fattura, the thing made. Line 5 ends on fattore, maker, answered by amore, love, and fiore, flower. This is terza rima, the chained rhyme Dante was the first to use for a long poem. Fattore and fattura come from one verb, to make. They end the lines that say the maker of human nature did not disdain to become its making. Maker then rhymes with love: line 7 says that in her womb love was lit again.
lenses.why: Maker and thing made, two words from one verb, end the lines that say the one became the other; maker then rhymes with love, the love that the next line says was lit again in her womb.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and lines 4 to 7. Terza rima and Dante’s first use of it: the Treccani *Vocabolario* under *terzina*, and the *Encyclopaedia Britannica* under *terza rima*. *Fattore* and *fattura*: the *Vocabolario*, whose entry for *fattura* cites these lines, and the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *fattura*.

grounds.source: Treccani, Vocabolario, terzina; Encyclopaedia Britannica, terza rima

(Examiner: the caption used to call fattura the maker’s word with the creature’s ending; no source says that, and fattura is the creature’s word. The sentence was cut.)

lenses.label: English

ties.say: The first pair crosses word for word.
The sense is whole. In Italian, daughter and son are one word with two endings, *figlia* and *figlio*. English has two unlike words.
The third pair is kept: *lowly* and *uplifted*.
In the verse *creatura* ends a line and sets a rhyme that lines 4 and 6 must meet. In prose the word sets nothing.
*Making* for *fattura*. Wicksteed keeps one root for the two words, as Dante does.
*Farsi* is *fare*, to make, turned on oneself: to make oneself, and so to become. It is the verb inside *fattore* and *fattura*. The English word *become* loses it.
The image crosses. The flower is the rose of the blessed, shown in cantos 30 and 31. For *germinato*, sprouted, Wicksteed has *unfolded*.

lenses.caption: Beside Dante’s lines is the English prose of Wicksteed, printed in 1899 facing the Italian. A student recalls that Auden’s class had to write out cantos of the Comedy from memory in this prose, this canto last. Auden wrote that the sound of a poem, with its rhythm, rhymes and puns, cannot be translated, and that what does not rest on the words themselves, such as an image, can be, to a degree. The three pairs cross into English whole, and Maker and making keep one root as fattore and fattura do. The rhyme is gone, and so is the one letter that parts figlia from figlio.
lenses.why: The class learned this canto in Wicksteed’s prose, and the prose bears out what Auden wrote of translation: what does not rest on the words themselves can cross, and rhyme and wordplay stay behind.
lenses.stands: The two versions as they stand side by side. The class and this prose: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall,” pp. 153–54; Auden on what can be translated: *The Dyer’s Hand*, pp. 23–24. *Farsi* and *germinato*: the Treccani *Vocabolario* under *fare* and *germinare*. The rose of the blessed: [canto 30](#/read/dante-temple/par-30:38) and the opening of [canto 31](#/read/dante-temple/par-31:0).

plates.heading: What he saw in the light: lines 82 to 90
plates.label: Dante

lenses.label: Figure
lenses.name: metaphor
lenses.plain: one thing spoken of as another
lenses.caption: Three words come from the making of books. Legato is the word for binding a book. Si squaderna is made from quaderno, a quire, the gathering of folded sheets from which a book is sewn; the verb says the quires lie apart. So the things of the universe are spoken of as the loose quires of a book, and in the depth of the light Dante sees them bound, with love, in one volume. This is the first thing he tells of what he saw.
lenses.why: Dante gives the first thing he saw in the light as a bound book, so the scattered things of the universe and the one volume are the same leaves, loose and sewn; they are bound, the line says, with love.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and lines 85 to 87; metaphor as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it. The book words: the Treccani *Vocabolario* under *legare*, *squadernare* (which explains these lines) and *quaderno*, and the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *squadernarsi*. That this is the first thing he reports seeing: Chiavacci Leonardi’s note to lines 85–87.

grounds.source: Silva Rhetoricae (rhetoric.byu.edu), metaphor

lenses.caption: Lines 85 to 87 are in a bookbinder’s words: legato, bound; volume; si squaderna, lies apart in quires. Lines 88 to 90 say it again in the terms of the schools of his day. Sustanze are things that exist in themselves, and accidenti the qualities that exist in them. Conflati is from a Latin verb for melting metals together. The sentence ends on un semplice lume, which is read two ways: the thing he speaks of is one light without parts, or what he says of it is no more than a glimmer. At line 55 he has said that from there on his sight was greater than speech shows.
lenses.why: Dante says one thing twice, in a bookbinder’s words and then in the terms of the schools, and ends on a phrase read as one light or a bare glimmer; he has said speech falls short of his sight.
lenses.stands: The Treccani *Vocabolario* under *internare*, *legare*, *volume*, *squadernare*, *quaderno* and *semplice*; Lewis and Short’s Latin dictionary under *volumen* and *conflo*; the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *internarsi* and *volume*. Substance, accident and the two readings of the last phrase: the notes of Sapegno, Singleton, Bosco and Reggio, and Chiavacci Leonardi to lines 88–90. In the poem: [line 55](#/read/dante-temple/par-33:18), [the Sibyl’s leaves](#/read/dante-temple/par-33:21) and [Virgil’s volume](#/read/dante-italian/inf-01:27).

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: Line 83 ends on etterna, eternal. In terza rima, the chained rhyme of this poem, its sound must come back twice, and the two words that bring it are verbs of opposite sense: s’interna, is held deep within, and si squaderna, lies apart in quires. One subject has both verbs. So the rhyme, which makes the end of a line stand out, sets there the gathered and the scattered state of the same things. The line between them ends on volume, and lume, light, the same word without its first two letters, answers it. Six times in the poem a line ends on the word for volume, and each time the word for light rhymes with it.
lenses.why: The chain’s rhyme sets at two line ends the verbs for being held within and for lying apart, said of the same things; the next rhyme has lume, light, inside volume, and the poem pairs the two every time.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and lines 85 to 87. The chain’s rule: the Treccani *Vocabolario* under *terzina*; the two verbs, under *internare* and *squadernare*. That rhyme underlines a line’s end: the *Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* under *rima*, and Baum, *The Principles of English Versification*, chapter 3. Counted in the Italian printed here: lines ending on the word for volume (*Inferno* 1.84; *Paradiso* 15.50, 23.112, 26.119, 28.14, 33.86).

plates.heading: The end of the poem: lines 139 to 145
plates.label: Dante

lenses.label: Sentence

spans.label: verbs: were not enough for this
what is turned: desire and will

lenses.caption: The last three lines make one statement, and its subject comes last. First the verb, volgeva, was turning; then what is turned, my desire and my will; then a wheel that is evenly moved. Only the last line names what turns them: l’amor, love. A sentence that holds back what completes its sense is called periodic; here that is the subject. In all seven lines no verb has Dante for its subject: his wings are not enough, his mind is struck, power fails. Auden gave the Comedy as his example of a quest in which the vision is given by grace and reached by no act of the dreamer.
lenses.why: Dante keeps the subject of the last statement, love, for the last line. In all seven lines no verb has him for its subject, and Auden says such a vision is reached by no act of the dreamer.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage, and the seven lines themselves. That the subject of the last statement is held for the last line: Singleton’s note to line 143. The periodic sentence as *Silva Rhetoricae* defines it, under *period*. Auden: “K.’s Quest,” in *The Kafka Problem*, pp. 47–48.

grounds.claim: the order of the last statement: verb, object, comparison, and the subject last; the subject and verb of each earlier clause

points.say: The last syllable of *fantasia* is the sixth of the line, and stressed. *Qui*, here, is the seventh, and can be heard stressed too: two more stresses together, at the middle of the line.
The last syllable of *mancò* and the first of *possa* are both stressed: the ninth and tenth of the line, with nothing unstressed between them.
Stress on syllables 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Twice a final vowel runs into the vowel that begins the next word, and a small arc ties the two. So thirteen written syllables count as eleven.

lenses.caption: Dante’s line has eleven syllables. The last accent always falls on the tenth and, as a rule, another on the fourth or the sixth. In Italian, stresses tend to fall on every second syllable, and verse tends to avoid two side by side. The last line keeps that pattern exactly. Line 142 ends on two stresses together: mancò possa, failed and power, its ninth syllable and its tenth. A stress on the ninth, a study of Dante’s verse says, strikes against the tenth and brings out the word it falls on. Here that word is mancò: power, the line says, failed his high fantasy, the faculty that receives images.
lenses.why: The line that says power failed ends on two stresses together, which Italian verse tends to avoid; a stress on the ninth brings out its word, here failed. The last line returns to a stress on every second syllable.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage: the stresses as one reader hears them, by the rules of the Italian line (*Enciclopedia dell’Italiano* and Treccani *Vocabolario*, under *endecasillabo*). Where stresses tend to fall: Luca Zuliani, “Sulla cesura dell’endecasillabo,” p. 173; Bruno Germano, *Il solfeggio dei versi*, p. 24. A stress on the ninth: *Enciclopedia Dantesca*, under *endecasillabo*, section 6. Fantasy as the faculty that receives images: Singleton’s note to line 142.

lenses.label: Rhyme
lenses.caption: In terza rima the middle line of each group of three gives the rhyme to the next group. So the chain cannot end on a group: its middle line would have no answer. Every canto ends on one line more. The word left waiting is velle, Latin for to will, used as a noun: his will. The line that answers it ends the poem on stelle, stars. The poem has velle twice, both times rhymed with stelle. Mossa, moved, the rhyme word before, returns in the last line as move, moves, the word that ends the first line of the Paradiso. Auden wrote that the poem’s structure fixes even the number of its lines; the rhyme scheme requires this one.
lenses.why: The middle rhyme of the last group of three needs one more line, so the form requires line 145; velle, his will, is answered by stelle, the stars, and the last line’s verb ends the Paradiso’s first line too.
lenses.stands: The marks on the passage; the closing line of the chain: the Treccani *Vocabolario* under *terzina*. *Velle* and *move*: the same dictionary under *velle* and *muovere*, and the *Enciclopedia Dantesca* under *velle*. Counted in the Italian printed here: every canto has a multiple of three lines, plus one; *velle* comes twice, here and in [canto 4](#/read/dante-italian/par-04:8); *move* ends the first line of [canto 1](#/read/dante-italian/par-01:0). Auden: *Forewords and Afterwords*, p. 269.

grounds.source: Treccani, Vocabolario, terzina

lenses.caption: The Comedy has 100 cantos: one to open the whole and 33 for each of three parts. Every canto is a chain of three-line groups closed by a single line. The parts run to 4,720, 4,755 and 4,758 lines. Auden speaks of a mathematical structure that fixes even the number of lines. At the end of the Purgatorio Dante says the pages laid out for that part are full, and the curb of art lets him go no further. Each part ends on stelle, stars: the Inferno on seeing them again, the Purgatorio on being ready to rise to them, the Paradiso on the love that moves them.
lenses.why: Each canto and the whole poem are built as threes with one over, and the three nearly equal parts end on one word; Auden speaks of a mathematical structure that fixes even the number of lines.

auden.says: In an essay on Kafka, Auden sorts the quests of literature into kinds and gives the *Comedy* as his example of the Dream Quest. The journey is after no object. It seeks knowledge of the spirit, a sight of what is real behind what appears, and the dreamer, awake again, can from then on live his earthly life. The dreamer stands for everyman. Seeing will not of itself change him, Auden adds, but one who has seen and stays the same has more to answer for than those who never saw.
auden.quote: it is not by any act or virtue of his that he attains this vision, for the vision is a gift of Divine Grace
auden.source: “K.’s Quest,” in *The Kafka Problem*, edited by Angel Flores (New York: New Directions, 1946), pp. 47–48

auden.says: In *New Year Letter*, published in the spring of 1941, before the course, Auden imagines himself on trial before a court of dead poets, and the judge who presides over his case is Dante. He draws him as a gaunt, weathered explorer who ruined his worldly prospects and gave his whole self, feeling, senses, will and thinking, to what lies beyond nature. With rational love for a guide he crossed Hell, Purgatory and Heaven, and he saw, exactly and in detail, all that surrounds and sustains the soul.
auden.source: *New Year Letter* (1941), Part 1; in *The Collected Poetry of W. H. Auden* (1945), pp. 269–70

auden.says: Donald Pearce, who took the course in 1941, describes the final examination. Auden told the class they would write out, from memory, seven of the *Comedy*’s cantos in the prose of Carlyle and Wicksteed, the version, he said, that Eliot used in *The Waste Land*. The list began with *Inferno* 3 and 5 and finished with this canto. When a committee of students called the task impossible he cut seven to five. Pearce says the last canto took him one afternoon to learn, and that in the examination he wrote without a stop for the full three hours. Others in the class remembered the number of cantos as six.
auden.source: Donald Pearce, “Fortunate Fall: W. H. Auden at Michigan,” in *W. H. Auden: The Far Interior*, edited by Alan Bold (1985), pp. 153–54; for the six cantos, Charles H. Miller, *Auden: An American Friendship* (1983), pp. 26–27 and 77–78

auden.says: Auden did not accept that poetry is simply what cannot be translated. What the words sound like, how they move, and whatever meaning hangs on sound, a rhyme or a pun, cannot be carried over. Pictures and comparisons taken from what the senses know can be, in part, and so can a poet’s own way of seeing the world. His test: put a poem of Goethe’s and one of Hölderlin’s into literal prose, and a reader can still tell that two different men wrote them.

caveats: The stresses are marked as one reader hears them, by the rules of the Italian line. A few syllables in lines 139 to 144 can be heard or counted another way. The captions lean only on the ninth and tenth syllables of line 142 and on the last line.

What a stress on the ninth syllable does is a general remark about Dante’s line in the *Enciclopedia Dantesca*. Line 142 is not among its examples: that the remark holds there is this page’s own application. No commentary read for this page marks the stresses of these lines.

Three meanings are disputed. The last phrase of line 90 is read as one simple light or as a mere glimmer. What *disio* and *velle* each name in line 143 is debated; here they are only desire and will. That *s’interna* also means *is threefold* is rejected by some commentators.

Auden’s remark is general: the poem’s structure, he says, dictates even the number of verses. That the closing line of each canto and the line counts are cases of it is this page’s reading. His essay “K.’s Quest” was read only in search extracts of a scanned copy.
That seven cantos were cut to five is one student’s memory, printed more than forty years later. Two others in the class remembered six. Only Pearce names this canto and the prose version.
open: The scansion of lines 139 to 145 is mine, made by the rules for the Italian eleven-syllable line. I found no commentary that scans these lines or remarks on the two stresses at the end of line 142.

Four syllables can be heard another way: the first stress of line 140 on its second syllable in place of the third; in line 141 the hiatus set between da and un (the hosted text prints no diaeresis on sua, and Dante counts da and un apart in Inferno 13.32); qui in line 142 without stress; sì in line 144 with stress. The captions lean only on the ninth and tenth syllables of line 142 and on the last line.

That stresses side by side slow a line is taken from a handbook of English verse. The Italian sources say only that stresses tend to fall every two syllables and that verse tends to avoid two in a row; one adds that a stress next to another carries emphasis. (Examiner: mended. The caption no longer says that meeting stresses slow the line. It gives what the Enciclopedia Dantesca says under endecasillabo, section 6: a prominent stress on the ninth strikes against the tenth and brings out its word. Line 142 is not among that article’s examples; the application is the page’s own, and a caveat says so.)

“K.’s Quest” was read in the research notes and in search snippets of a restricted scan; the page was not seen whole. The lines of New Year Letter on Dante were read only in the research notes. (Examiner: the lines of New Year Letter have now been read in the text of the 1945 Collected Poetry, pp. 269–70. “K.’s Quest” is still known only from search extracts of the restricted scan, and a caveat says so; a page marker 48 in the extract stands just before the quoted sentence.)
The scan of Forewords and Afterwords drops most punctuation. The quotation in the view keeps the scan’s one comma and sets in lower case a word the scan prints in capitals.

Un semplice lume (line 90) is read two ways. Longfellow and Wicksteed take it as one simple light; the Treccani dictionary and the recent commentaries take it as a mere glimmer of what he saw. The captions give both.
S’interna (line 85): that the word also means to be threefold is a reading of some commentators which others reject. It is given in a note as a possibility only.

The Italian commentaries call the three pairs of lines 1 and 2 antitheses. Paradox is my choice of English term for them; it fits the definition, and one commentary in English calls them paradoxical expressions.
What disio and velle each mean in line 143 is disputed among the commentaries. The reading gives them only as desire and will.
Auden’s remark on a structure that fixes the number of verses is general. That the single closing line of each canto and the line counts are instances of it is my application, not his.
How many cantos the class learned differs with the witness: six in most accounts, seven cut to five in Pearce, eight in another. Only Pearce names this canto and the prose version.

The volume in which Zuliani’s article appeared is known to me only from a search result; the page was read in a PDF of the article. (Examiner: settled. The contents page of the volume itself, Interruzioni e cesure, edited by Raffaele Donnarumma and Francesca Romoli, Pisa University Press, 2021, has Zuliani’s essay at p. 165 and the next at p. 177.)
Examiner: the Encyclopaedia Britannica articles (The Divine Comedy; terza rima) would not open from here and were read in copies kept by the Wayback Machine.
